newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian rupiah weathers peso devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian rupiah weathers peso devaluation.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah has benefited from sound economic fundamentals and emerged relatively unscathed following speculative attacks on the Philippines peso and Thai baht, economists said on Friday.
Prudent monetary and fiscal management and early pre-emptive central bank moves such as a widening in the dollar-rupiah band seemed to have safeguarded the rupiah, the economists said.
"People aren't really worried about the contagion effects of either the Thai baht and now the Philippine peso on the rupiah," said Daragh Maher, economist at Ing Barings.
Maher said stable economic growth, the long-term nature of foreign debt and controllable short-term private debt have helped shield the rupiah from speculation.
Central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said short-term loans of less than one year accounted for only 9.1 percent, or $9.1 billion, of the total foreign loans of $109.3 billion.
"I'm pretty comfortable with the rupiah. Any spillover is only temporary," Maher said, referring to a brief jolt in the rupiah after the peso was freed into a wider range.
The Philippine Central Bank said on Friday that the peso was allowed to move in a wider range against the dollar, making it the second Asian currency beaten by speculators in two weeks.
Thailand introduced a managed float of the baht last week after its currency came under continuous pressure.
But the rupiah was relatively unharmed compared to other regional currencies, weakening only to 2,437.0 to the dollar from an opening of 2,433.0 on Friday after the peso announcement.
The rupiah lost less than half a percent last week on the spillover effects from the Thai baht float, but it soon recovered to trade in the stronger end of the central bank's intervention band.
Since 1992, the central bank has widened the intervention band in steps to give more room for price fluctuations and absorb shocks. It now has an eight percent band.
Saleh Aziz, treasury manager of the PT Bank Ekspor Impor Indonesia, said the government had taken steps to reduce any shocks to the local currency.

He said an economic reform package announced last Monday with tariff cuts on 1,600 items and loan curbs on property developers helped maintain Indonesia's growth momentum and address concerns in the property sector.
"That makes us better prepared to face any eventuality."
The World bank had said Indonesia was losing its deregulation momentum and warned against rising exposure of the banking industry to the property sector.
Aziz predicted the rupiah would return to the strong end of the intervention band after the dust in the region settled.
Maher said his view on Indonesia remained unchanged, and any further rupiah turbulence would be short-lived.

"Economic growth is very stable. It hasn't been cyclical. More importantly, the nature of financing is long-term rather than short-term," he said, adding that capital entering the country was foreign direct investments rather than portfolio flows.
"There has not been a big accumulation of short-term debts by the private sector that we have had in Thailand," he said.
Foreign direct investments were $15.47 billion in the first six months against $20.96 billion in the same 1996 period.
"You will get some $25 billion for the full year. It's relative to the current account deficit of say $10 billion. You are not running into dangerous levels," Maher said.
